title: Active-Active
subtitle: Concurrent multi-region writes, conflict resolution models (LWW vs CRDTs), and capacity headroom.
keyTakeaways: In an active-active setup, multiple regions process reads and writes concurrently, removing the need for manual regional failover while demanding clear strategies for write conflicts.
Concurrent writes without global consensus inevitably diverge; teams resolve this using Last-Write-Wins (risk of silent data overwrites), CRDTs (for counters/sets), or strict home-region sharding.
Active-active requires significant capacity headroom: if you operate two regions, each must run at under 50% utilization so a single regional failure does not overwhelm the surviving region.

sections.heading: Multi-Master Write Conflicts and Convergence Models
sections.body: When two regions accept writes without synchronous cross-region locks, modifications to the same record within the replication window (roughly 50 to 200ms across continents) create divergent state. Resolving these write-write conflicts requires selecting the right consistency and merge strategy for your data model.
bullets: Last-Write-Wins (LWW) risks: LWW resolves collisions by taking the write with the highest timestamp. However, NTP clock drift across cloud instances (often 10 to 50ms) means a write executed later in physical time can be discarded by an earlier write with a drifted forward timestamp.

Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs): State-based or operation-based CRDTs (like PN-Counters for inventory reserves, LWW-Element-Sets for user carts, or Observed-Removed Sets) guarantee that all regions converge to the exact same state once all mutations replicate, without manual conflict intervention.

Home-region sharding: The cleanest way to avoid write conflicts is to partition users by home region. A user in Europe writes only to `eu-west-1`. If they travel to the US, their writes are proxied back to their home region or the home region is migrated explicitly.

sections.heading: Traffic Evacuation, Capacity Headroom, and Failover Drills
sections.body: A key benefit of active-active over active-passive is eliminating failover hesitation. Because every region handles real customer traffic 24/7, caches are warm, connection pools are primed, and network paths are continuously verified.
bullets: The capacity headroom rule: In a two-region active-active deployment, each region must operate below 50% CPU and database capacity during normal operations. If Region A fails and Region B is already running at 75% load, shifting 100% of traffic to Region B will immediately crash it via resource exhaustion.

N+1 regional sizing: In a three-region active-active deployment, each region runs at ~33% normal capacity (or 66% if sized for N-1 redundancy). As you scale to more regions, the cost overhead of redundant headroom decreases.

Fast traffic drainage: Use BGP Anycast withdrawal or low-TTL DNS weighted records (TTL = 10 to 30s) to drain traffic away from an unhealthy region in seconds, redirecting incoming requests to the surviving healthy sites.

tradeOffs.pros: Eliminates cross-region write conflicts completely; delivers sub-10ms local write latency for users in their home zone.
tradeOffs.cons: Cross-region interactions (like transfers between users in different regions) require distributed sagas; roaming users pay WAN latency.
tradeOffs.bestFor: SaaS platforms, e-commerce user profiles, and regional banking applications.

tradeOffs.pros: Allows any user to write to any healthy region anytime; near-zero RTO during regional network partitions.
tradeOffs.cons: Restricted data types (counters, sets, registers); cannot easily enforce global invariants like unique username constraints.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Social engagement metrics (likes, view counts), collaborative shopping carts, and distributed metric counters.

interviewTip: When recommending active-active in an interview, do not forget the capacity math: explain that if two regions share load equally, each region must run below 50% capacity so that when one region goes down, the other can absorb 100% of global traffic without collapsing.
